details.account: This agent adds an AppWorld-specific operational skill, a reformatted `appworld_execute` tool, and a final-answer verification middleware on top of the baseline ReAct loop. The skill forces API orientation (`print(dir(apis))`), small incremental code experiments, explicit printing of observed values, and not finalizing while the latest shell result reports `TASK_COMPLETED: false`. The tool parses the shell's JSON reply and prominently surfaces `OUTPUT` and `TASK_COMPLETED` instead of returning compact raw JSON. The `verify_final` middleware remembers full recent AppWorld results, hard-refuses final answers when the most recent relevant result says `TASK_COMPLETED: false`, and otherwise asks a side LLM verifier to either accept the answer or send the agent back with one specific missing-evidence instruction. I expect higher accuracy because this prevents premature or unsupported final answers and steers the agent toward evidence-gathering and observed API discovery rather than hallucinated AppWorld calls.

This agent keeps the previous AppWorld skill, reformatted `appworld_execute` tool, and final-answer verifier, and adds two new middlewares. `api_guard` statically inspects each `appworld_execute` snippet before execution, learns top-level API names from `print(dir(apis))` output, and skips any direct `apis.<name>` call whose top-level name has not been observed; if parsing is ambiguous it falls back to permissive mode so it cannot deadlock. `autodebug` detects Python tracebacks and injects one bounded, side-LLM-generated read-only diagnostic snippet (dir/type/get/print) as an extra tool call in the same turn, so common errors are diagnosed without spending a main-loop turn or retrying side-effecting operations. The skill and tool description were updated to tell the model about both behaviors. I expect higher accuracy because fewer hallucinated API names and faster recovery from bad calls give the final verifier cleaner, more complete observed evidence.

This agent wraps the raw AppWorld shell in orient-before-acting middleware and an enforced completion gate. `api_guard` blocks direct `apis.<name>` calls until `print(dir(apis))` has been observed and parsed, preventing hallucinated top-level service names. `autodoc` then uses a side LLM to choose 1-3 task-relevant `apis.api_docs` search queries and injects one same-turn read-only call that prints app descriptions plus compact matching API docs (app, API name, description, parameter names/types). `autodebug` injects a single read-only diagnostic after tracebacks so the main agent sees the fix without re-running side effects. Finally, the skill, system prompt, tool description, and `verify_final` make completion explicit end-to-end: `verify_final` refuses to finalize unless the latest AppWorld result reports `TASK_COMPLETED: true`, directing the model to call `apis.supervisor.complete_task(answer=...)` and wait for that result. I expect higher accuracy because the agent learns exact API and argument names before writing side-effecting calls, recovers from tracebacks without repeating them, and cannot stop until the AppWorld supervisor actually marks the task complete.

This agent keeps the orient-before-acting API guard, autodoc, autodebug, and final-answer gate, and adds two layers of early verification.

First, api_guard is extended from top-level service names to method-level calls: once `dir(apis.<app>)` has been printed and parsed, any direct `apis.<app>.<method>` not in that listing is skipped before execution, so hallucinated methods are blocked the same way hallucinated top-level apps already were. `apis.supervisor.complete_task` is still left to the completion path, and the guard stays permissive when dir output could not be parsed.

Second, a new pre_complete middleware intercepts `apis.supervisor.complete_task(...)` before it executes and asks a side LLM verifier whether the proposed answer is directly supported by observed tool outputs and whether all requested actions have observed evidence. If not, the call is skipped with one specific missing-evidence instruction, forcing the agent to print/verify the missing value or action before marking the task complete. The check is conservative: it allows on JSON parse failure, after a small number of blocks, and for injected read-only calls, so a noisy verifier cannot deadlock the run.

I expect higher accuracy because wrong answers and premature completions are caught before the supervisor state is mutated, and hallucinated methods are blocked before any side effects, while the conservative fallbacks keep the guard from stalling a recoverable run.

This agent adapts the MiniAgent runtime to AppWorld and layers five middlewares around the persistent-shell tool. `api_guard` records the top-level APIs observed from `print(dir(apis))` and blocks direct `apis.<name>` calls for unobserved names, preventing guessed API surfaces. `autodoc` then injects one read-only `apis.api_docs` lookup so the model sees relevant app/API names and parameters without spending a turn. `task_plan` asks a side LLM for a short goal/checklist grounded in the task and injects it before the next main-model turn, reducing omitted sub-actions or required values. `autodebug` turns tracebacks into one side-LLM diagnostic snippet, now with a deterministic AST check that rejects syntactically invalid or obviously side-effecting code before injection, so recovery does not retry sends/writes/payments. `verify_final` keeps a compact ledger of recent AppWorld results and literal `apis.supervisor.complete_task(answer=...)` values, refuses to finalize until a recent AppWorld result reports `TASK_COMPLETED: true` (bounded by the runtime's final-continue cap so runs cannot deadlock), then asks a side verifier to accept, send one specific missing-evidence instruction, or replace the answer with a tightened exact string matching observed outputs and the submitted supervisor answer. I expect higher accuracy because early planning prevents skipped actions, API/doc guardrails reduce failed calls, error recovery avoids wasted turns without side effects, and final answers are pinned to observed evidence rather than verbose or mismatched strings, while JSON/LLM fallbacks keep the gates from deadlocking runs.

This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two new pieces. First, a deterministic `memory` middleware builds a non-blocking working-memory board: it parses `print(dir(apis))`, `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, and `apis.api_docs` output, then injects only newly observed facts before the next turn as a `[memory update]` — new top-level apps, per-app methods, and exact signatures like `apis.email.send_email(to: str, subject: str)`. This keeps exact API/argument names in front of the model without the aggressive blocking that made the earlier method-level guard hurt. Second, `verify_final` now distinguishes an explicit `TASK_COMPLETED: false`: instead of only returning a generic "keep working" message, it asks a small side-LLM coach for the single most important missing action or verification grounded in the task and recent tool outputs, with the generic message as fallback. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly forgotten signatures/hallucinated parameters and omitted multi-step sub-actions, and these two changes target exactly those failure modes while preserving the guardrails that already worked.

This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting `api_guard`, broad top-level `autodoc`, traceback-driven `autodebug`, and the `TASK_COMPLETED: true` final gate) and adds a new `method_docs` middleware. After the main agent successfully inspects a concrete app with `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, `method_docs` injects one read-only `apis.api_docs.search_api_docs(query=<app>)` call in the same turn, so the model sees that app's method names, descriptions, and parameter names/types before it writes the next side-effecting call. It is deliberately conservative: it fires only for direct `apis.<app>` dir calls whose output parsed as a real identifier list, skips traceback results so autodebug keeps the injection slot, skips `api_docs`/`supervisor`, caps total injections, deduplicates apps, and respects the runtime's one-injection-per-turn rule so it cannot collide with autodoc/autodebug or recurse. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures after top-level orientation are mostly hallucinated app-specific method and argument names, and this targets exactly that gap with read-only documentation instead of a blocking method-level guard.

This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two deterministic last-mile guardrails. First, a new `supervisor_answer` middleware records the exact `answer=` value submitted to `apis.supervisor.complete_task`; when the latest real AppWorld shell result says `TASK_COMPLETED: true`, it replaces the model's free-text final answer with that exact submitted value. For non-literal answer expressions it injects one read-only `print(repr(<expr>))` capture and pins the observed scalar value, while never treating middleware skip text as evidence of a submitted answer. Second, a new `repeat_guard` middleware skips an immediate exact repeat of any snippet that just raised a traceback, and any subsequent successful shell result clears the guard so valid retries are never permanently blocked. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly last-mile answer mismatches and stuck-loop repetitions: pinning the final answer to the supervisor-accepted value eliminates verbose or paraphrased answers, and the repeat guard prevents the agent from burning turns re-running a snippet it already knows fails.

This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two things.

First, a documentation-backed argument guard (`param_guard`) learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print (`## app | api` and `  - name | type | required= ...` lines). Before executing a direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call for which it has a signature, it skips the call if it uses a keyword argument absent from the documented parameter list or omits a documented required argument, and it shows the exact signature. It stays conservative: it never blocks unobserved signatures, `*`/`**` unpacking, `api_docs`/`supervisor`, or injected read-only calls, and it caps total blocks so parser noise cannot deadlock the run. This targets hallucinated parameter names and omitted required arguments just before side effects, without the method-level blocking that previously hurt.

Second, `verify_final` keeps a de-duplicated evidence ledger of short stdout lines from every real AppWorld result, while excluding API-doc output (app descriptions, `## app | api` doc sections, parameter lines, and doc-search markers) and middleware skip text. The final side verifier sees that whole ledger in addition to recent calls, so an answer is not accepted unsupported or rejected merely because the confirming output scrolled out of the recent-call window.

I expect a higher score because after method_docs the remaining failures are wrong call arguments and last-mile verification gaps; this design blocks the former only when the docs make the error deterministic, and gives the verifier the full observed-evidence trail for the latter.

This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds a reactive `arg_repair` middleware. It learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print, and when a later direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call raises an argument-binding TypeError (unexpected keyword, missing required argument, wrong positional count, or multiple values), a side LLM proposes a corrected same-call snippet. The repair is injected in the same turn only after deterministic AST validation: it must be the same single `apis.<app>.<method>` call path, use only documented keyword parameter names, supply every required parameter, and add no other `apis.*` call or `getattr(apis, ...)`. I expect a higher score because this directly fixes the remaining hallucinated-parameter and omitted-required-argument failures after method_docs, but unlike a blocking param_guard it never stalls valid work — it only retries calls that Python already proved failed during argument binding, before the function body could run, and it rejects any extra `apis.*` call so AppWorld actions are not duplicated.

entries.account: This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two new pieces. First, a deterministic `memory` middleware builds a non-blocking working-memory board: it parses `print(dir(apis))`, `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, and `apis.api_docs` output, then injects only newly observed facts before the next turn as a `[memory update]` — new top-level apps, per-app methods, and exact signatures like `apis.email.send_email(to: str, subject: str)`. This keeps exact API/argument names in front of the model without the aggressive blocking that made the earlier method-level guard hurt. Second, `verify_final` now distinguishes an explicit `TASK_COMPLETED: false`: instead of only returning a generic "keep working" message, it asks a small side-LLM coach for the single most important missing action or verification grounded in the task and recent tool outputs, with the generic message as fallback. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly forgotten signatures/hallucinated parameters and omitted multi-step sub-actions, and these two changes target exactly those failure modes while preserving the guardrails that already worked.

entries.account: This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting `api_guard`, broad top-level `autodoc`, traceback-driven `autodebug`, and the `TASK_COMPLETED: true` final gate) and adds a new `method_docs` middleware. After the main agent successfully inspects a concrete app with `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, `method_docs` injects one read-only `apis.api_docs.search_api_docs(query=<app>)` call in the same turn, so the model sees that app's method names, descriptions, and parameter names/types before it writes the next side-effecting call. It is deliberately conservative: it fires only for direct `apis.<app>` dir calls whose output parsed as a real identifier list, skips traceback results so autodebug keeps the injection slot, skips `api_docs`/`supervisor`, caps total injections, deduplicates apps, and respects the runtime's one-injection-per-turn rule so it cannot collide with autodoc/autodebug or recurse. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures after top-level orientation are mostly hallucinated app-specific method and argument names, and this targets exactly that gap with read-only documentation instead of a blocking method-level guard.

entries.account: This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two deterministic last-mile guardrails. First, a new `supervisor_answer` middleware records the exact `answer=` value submitted to `apis.supervisor.complete_task`; when the latest real AppWorld shell result says `TASK_COMPLETED: true`, it replaces the model's free-text final answer with that exact submitted value. For non-literal answer expressions it injects one read-only `print(repr(<expr>))` capture and pins the observed scalar value, while never treating middleware skip text as evidence of a submitted answer. Second, a new `repeat_guard` middleware skips an immediate exact repeat of any snippet that just raised a traceback, and any subsequent successful shell result clears the guard so valid retries are never permanently blocked. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly last-mile answer mismatches and stuck-loop repetitions: pinning the final answer to the supervisor-accepted value eliminates verbose or paraphrased answers, and the repeat guard prevents the agent from burning turns re-running a snippet it already knows fails.

This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two things.

First, a documentation-backed argument guard (`param_guard`) learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print (`## app | api` and `  - name | type | required= ...` lines). Before executing a direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call for which it has a signature, it skips the call if it uses a keyword argument absent from the documented parameter list or omits a documented required argument, and it shows the exact signature. It stays conservative: it never blocks unobserved signatures, `*`/`**` unpacking, `api_docs`/`supervisor`, or injected read-only calls, and it caps total blocks so parser noise cannot deadlock the run. This targets hallucinated parameter names and omitted required arguments just before side effects, without the method-level blocking that previously hurt.

Second, `verify_final` keeps a de-duplicated evidence ledger of short stdout lines from every real AppWorld result, while excluding API-doc output (app descriptions, `## app | api` doc sections, parameter lines, and doc-search markers) and middleware skip text. The final side verifier sees that whole ledger in addition to recent calls, so an answer is not accepted unsupported or rejected merely because the confirming output scrolled out of the recent-call window.

I expect a higher score because after method_docs the remaining failures are wrong call arguments and last-mile verification gaps; this design blocks the former only when the docs make the error deterministic, and gives the verifier the full observed-evidence trail for the latter.

entries.account: This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds a reactive `arg_repair` middleware. It learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print, and when a later direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call raises an argument-binding TypeError (unexpected keyword, missing required argument, wrong positional count, or multiple values), a side LLM proposes a corrected same-call snippet. The repair is injected in the same turn only after deterministic AST validation: it must be the same single `apis.<app>.<method>` call path, use only documented keyword parameter names, supply every required parameter, and add no other `apis.*` call or `getattr(apis, ...)`. I expect a higher score because this directly fixes the remaining hallucinated-parameter and omitted-required-argument failures after method_docs, but unlike a blocking param_guard it never stalls valid work — it only retries calls that Python already proved failed during argument binding, before the function body could run, and it rejects any extra `apis.*` call so AppWorld actions are not duplicated.

designs.account: This agent adds an AppWorld-specific operational skill, a reformatted `appworld_execute` tool, and a final-answer verification middleware on top of the baseline ReAct loop. The skill forces API orientation (`print(dir(apis))`), small incremental code experiments, explicit printing of observed values, and not finalizing while the latest shell result reports `TASK_COMPLETED: false`. The tool parses the shell's JSON reply and prominently surfaces `OUTPUT` and `TASK_COMPLETED` instead of returning compact raw JSON. The `verify_final` middleware remembers full recent AppWorld results, hard-refuses final answers when the most recent relevant result says `TASK_COMPLETED: false`, and otherwise asks a side LLM verifier to either accept the answer or send the agent back with one specific missing-evidence instruction. I expect higher accuracy because this prevents premature or unsupported final answers and steers the agent toward evidence-gathering and observed API discovery rather than hallucinated AppWorld calls.

designs.account:
This agent keeps the orient-before-acting API guard, autodoc, autodebug, and final-answer gate, and adds two layers of early verification.

First, api_guard is extended from top-level service names to method-level calls: once `dir(apis.<app>)` has been printed and parsed, any direct `apis.<app>.<method>` not in that listing is skipped before execution, so hallucinated methods are blocked the same way hallucinated top-level apps already were. `apis.supervisor.complete_task` is still left to the completion path, and the guard stays permissive when dir output could not be parsed.

Second, a new pre_complete middleware intercepts `apis.supervisor.complete_task(...)` before it executes and asks a side LLM verifier whether the proposed answer is directly supported by observed tool outputs and whether all requested actions have observed evidence. If not, the call is skipped with one specific missing-evidence instruction, forcing the agent to print/verify the missing value or action before marking the task complete. The check is conservative: it allows on JSON parse failure, after a small number of blocks, and for injected read-only calls, so a noisy verifier cannot deadlock the run.

I expect higher accuracy because wrong answers and premature completions are caught before the supervisor state is mutated, and hallucinated methods are blocked before any side effects, while the conservative fallbacks keep the guard from stalling a recoverable run.

designs.account: This agent adapts the MiniAgent runtime to AppWorld and layers five middlewares around the persistent-shell tool. `api_guard` records the top-level APIs observed from `print(dir(apis))` and blocks direct `apis.<name>` calls for unobserved names, preventing guessed API surfaces. `autodoc` then injects one read-only `apis.api_docs` lookup so the model sees relevant app/API names and parameters without spending a turn. `task_plan` asks a side LLM for a short goal/checklist grounded in the task and injects it before the next main-model turn, reducing omitted sub-actions or required values. `autodebug` turns tracebacks into one side-LLM diagnostic snippet, now with a deterministic AST check that rejects syntactically invalid or obviously side-effecting code before injection, so recovery does not retry sends/writes/payments. `verify_final` keeps a compact ledger of recent AppWorld results and literal `apis.supervisor.complete_task(answer=...)` values, refuses to finalize until a recent AppWorld result reports `TASK_COMPLETED: true` (bounded by the runtime's final-continue cap so runs cannot deadlock), then asks a side verifier to accept, send one specific missing-evidence instruction, or replace the answer with a tightened exact string matching observed outputs and the submitted supervisor answer. I expect higher accuracy because early planning prevents skipped actions, API/doc guardrails reduce failed calls, error recovery avoids wasted turns without side effects, and final answers are pinned to observed evidence rather than verbose or mismatched strings, while JSON/LLM fallbacks keep the gates from deadlocking runs.

designs.account: This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two new pieces. First, a deterministic `memory` middleware builds a non-blocking working-memory board: it parses `print(dir(apis))`, `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, and `apis.api_docs` output, then injects only newly observed facts before the next turn as a `[memory update]` — new top-level apps, per-app methods, and exact signatures like `apis.email.send_email(to: str, subject: str)`. This keeps exact API/argument names in front of the model without the aggressive blocking that made the earlier method-level guard hurt. Second, `verify_final` now distinguishes an explicit `TASK_COMPLETED: false`: instead of only returning a generic "keep working" message, it asks a small side-LLM coach for the single most important missing action or verification grounded in the task and recent tool outputs, with the generic message as fallback. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly forgotten signatures/hallucinated parameters and omitted multi-step sub-actions, and these two changes target exactly those failure modes while preserving the guardrails that already worked.

designs.account: This agent keeps the strong AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting `api_guard`, broad top-level `autodoc`, traceback-driven `autodebug`, and the `TASK_COMPLETED: true` final gate) and adds a new `method_docs` middleware. After the main agent successfully inspects a concrete app with `print(dir(apis.<app>))`, `method_docs` injects one read-only `apis.api_docs.search_api_docs(query=<app>)` call in the same turn, so the model sees that app's method names, descriptions, and parameter names/types before it writes the next side-effecting call. It is deliberately conservative: it fires only for direct `apis.<app>` dir calls whose output parsed as a real identifier list, skips traceback results so autodebug keeps the injection slot, skips `api_docs`/`supervisor`, caps total injections, deduplicates apps, and respects the runtime's one-injection-per-turn rule so it cannot collide with autodoc/autodebug or recurse. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures after top-level orientation are mostly hallucinated app-specific method and argument names, and this targets exactly that gap with read-only documentation instead of a blocking method-level guard.

designs.account: This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two deterministic last-mile guardrails. First, a new `supervisor_answer` middleware records the exact `answer=` value submitted to `apis.supervisor.complete_task`; when the latest real AppWorld shell result says `TASK_COMPLETED: true`, it replaces the model's free-text final answer with that exact submitted value. For non-literal answer expressions it injects one read-only `print(repr(<expr>))` capture and pins the observed scalar value, while never treating middleware skip text as evidence of a submitted answer. Second, a new `repeat_guard` middleware skips an immediate exact repeat of any snippet that just raised a traceback, and any subsequent successful shell result clears the guard so valid retries are never permanently blocked. I expect a higher score because the remaining failures are mostly last-mile answer mismatches and stuck-loop repetitions: pinning the final answer to the supervisor-accepted value eliminates verbose or paraphrased answers, and the repeat guard prevents the agent from burning turns re-running a snippet it already knows fails.

designs.account:
This agent keeps the proven AppWorld pipeline (orient-before-acting api_guard, autodoc, method_docs, autodebug, and the TASK_COMPLETED final gate) and adds two things.

First, a documentation-backed argument guard (`param_guard`) learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print (`## app | api` and `  - name | type | required= ...` lines). Before executing a direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call for which it has a signature, it skips the call if it uses a keyword argument absent from the documented parameter list or omits a documented required argument, and it shows the exact signature. It stays conservative: it never blocks unobserved signatures, `*`/`**` unpacking, `api_docs`/`supervisor`, or injected read-only calls, and it caps total blocks so parser noise cannot deadlock the run. This targets hallucinated parameter names and omitted required arguments just before side effects, without the method-level blocking that previously hurt.

Second, `verify_final` keeps a de-duplicated evidence ledger of short stdout lines from every real AppWorld result, while excluding API-doc output (app descriptions, `## app | api` doc sections, parameter lines, and doc-search markers) and middleware skip text. The final side verifier sees that whole ledger in addition to recent calls, so an answer is not accepted unsupported or rejected merely because the confirming output scrolled out of the recent-call window.

It learns exact method signatures from the `apis.api_docs` output that autodoc/method_docs already print, and when a later direct `apis.<app>.<method>(...)` call raises an argument-binding TypeError (unexpected keyword, missing required argument, wrong positional count, or multiple values), a side LLM proposes a corrected same-call snippet. details.account: This design adds a small stdio MCP bridge over the persistent AppWorld shell, launched with system Python. It keeps an `appworld_execute` escape hatch for arbitrary multi-step Python, but replaces the baseline's hand-written recurring snippets with validated, single-purpose tools: `appworld_task` (active task plus supervisor profile/addresses/cards/passwords), `appworld_api_docs` (app-level or single-API docs), `appworld_call` (one `apis[app][api](**params)` call), and `appworld_complete` (success/fail with typed scalar or list answers). The paired CLAUDE.md workflow forces read-task-first, consult-docs-before-calling, verify-state-before-finishing, and finish-once behavior. This should reduce the baseline's observed failures—missed supervisor credentials, wrong API arguments, and forgotten `supervisor.complete_task`—while still allowing batched multi-step loops through `execute`.

This agent keeps the AppWorld MCP bridge but adds a server-enforced, fail-closed completion gate. `appworld_audit` returns the active instruction plus the last 30 API calls, and `appworld_complete` is rejected unless a successful `appworld_audit` was the immediately preceding world-executing tool; a failed audit, or a complete attempt that reaches the world and fails, clears the gate so completion cannot proceed without a fresh audit. Direct `supervisor.complete_task` is blocked in both `appworld_call` and `appworld_execute`, and completion always submits status "success" with answers restricted to AppWorld's actual `AnswerType` (string/number/null only, with yes/no/true/false as strings rather than JSON booleans/lists/objects). `appworld_apps` and `appworld_search_docs` make API discovery cheaper and less error-prone, and the prompt reserves the final two shell interactions for audit and complete. This targets the remaining failures—premature or incomplete finishing and answer-format mistakes—by forcing a fresh instruction-vs-action-log check and rejecting invalid completion calls.

This design keeps the open AppWorld MCP bridge (execute/call/task/docs/complete) but makes it self-correcting before submission. A UserPromptSubmit hook attaches to the same AppWorld socket and injects the active instruction plus supervisor profile/addresses/cards/passwords before the first turn, so the agent never starts blind or spends a turn re-fetching credentials. `appworld_call` now enriches API failures with the documented parameter schema (when available) plus the Python signature and traceback, and it resolves apps/APIs by attribute access with item-access fallback, so wrong arguments are corrected immediately and calls work regardless of how the shell exposes `apis`. A new advisory `appworld_answer_check` echoes the active instruction and, if the task exposes an `answer_type`, returns a MATCH/MISMATCH verdict against the proposed answer's JSON type; when no `answer_type` is exposed it says so and gives type-inference guidance instead of blocking. Completion stays fail-open: `appworld_complete` calls `supervisor.complete_task` directly with only the answer (no unsupported status argument), and no answer-type restriction prevents finishing. CLAUDE.md now requires answer-check for question tasks and explicit state verification before finishing, while treating missing `task_type`/`answer_type` as inference problems rather than hard dependencies. I expect higher scores because it removes the failure modes of the audit-gate design (blocked completion, missed credentials, unsupported completion arguments) and catches malformed or typeless final answers before they are graded.

This design keeps the proven fail-open MCP bridge (single socket, execute/call/task/complete) and adds a read-only in-memory session recorder plus an `appworld_audit` tool returning the active instruction and the last 30 interactions with success/error outcomes. The audit is purely advisory and never blocks `appworld_complete`, avoiding the failure mode of the earlier audit-gate design. It also adds `appworld_apps`, `appworld_search_docs`, `appworld_api_docs`, and `appworld_inspect` for cheap app/API discovery and exact Python signatures before calls, and makes `appworld_call` attach signature, docstring, and a short traceback on failure. The workflow orients with task+apps, discovers/inspects before calling, verifies state with read APIs, then self-audits against the instruction before one fail-open `appworld_complete`; yes/no answers are submitted as strings. I expect it to score higher than the simple bridge because it catches skipped or failed steps and wrong API arguments before submission without reintroducing a completion gate, and without the noisy hook/answer-type checking that hurt the self-correcting design.

This agent keeps the proven fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge (execute/call/task/docs/complete) but makes completion self-normalizing only where AppWorld actually rejects an answer. `appworld_complete` converts JSON booleans into yes/no (or true/false when the instruction asks true/false) and joins lists in grader order with " | "; `None`, numbers, and strings now pass through unchanged so AppWorld's own grader rounds/strips/lowercases them exactly once, avoiding double-normalization. `appworld_task` also returns a short app catalog alongside the task and supervisor credentials in one call. It stays fail-open with no audit gate or extra pre-submit tool call, so it repairs the simple bridge's completion-format failures without the noise, blocking, or extra interactions that hurt the audit-gate and self-correcting designs.

This design keeps the fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge (`appworld_execute`/`appworld_call`/`appworld_task`/`appworld_api_docs`/`appworld_complete`) but fixes the false assumption that the supervisor API exposes `task_type`/`answer_type`. Instead, `appworld_task` returns the active instruction plus an `inferred_answer_type` computed from that instruction's wording, and `appworld_complete` fetches the active task once inside the same completion call and applies the same wording-derived inference. It converts only shapes AppWorld would reject or misread: JSON booleans become yes/no (or true/false when the instruction asks for true/false), boolean-word strings and 0/1 are aligned for yes/no or true/false questions, booleans become 1/0 for numeric questions, and lists are sorted/joined exactly like the grader. Ordinary numbers, strings, and None pass through so AppWorld's grader normalizes them exactly once. There is still no separate answer-check tool and no pre-submit gate. I expect this to score higher because it removes residual answer-shape mismatches without depending on nonexistent task metadata and without reintroducing noisy hooks, blocking audits, or extra model-facing answer-check interactions.

This agent keeps the fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and the leader's answer normalization, but adds `appworld_preview_complete`: a non-terminal dry-run of `appworld_complete` that performs the same normalization and returns the active instruction, the exact `submitted_answer`, its Python type, and the grader-normalized `grader_text` without calling `supervisor.complete_task`. CLAUDE.md now requires question tasks to preview the final answer, verify it against the instruction, fix and re-preview if needed, and only then commit once. Actual completion also echoes `submitted_answer`/`grader_text` for post-submit audit. This targets the last unrecoverable failure—a malformed or wrong-format final answer committed before the agent can react—without reintroducing fail-closed gates, noisy answer-type hooks, or blocking audits; the preview is fail-open and costs at most one extra interaction, which the workflow allows the model to skip when interactions are nearly exhausted.

This agent keeps the leader's fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and scalar answer normalization, and adds two non-intrusive improvements. First, every tool result is prefixed with the live world-call budget (e.g. [world call 4/30; 26 left]), so the model can pace long tasks, batch reads, or finish before the 30-interaction limit without spending an extra tool call to check. Second, appworld_complete accepts list/dict answers and, rather than relying only on a copied normalizer, imports AppWorld's real answer_to_text from the live appworld package, spot-checks it on a small list and None, and uses it for non-scalar answers; if that import or spot-check fails it falls back to the same conservative copied normalizer. Booleans are still converted exactly as before, and None, numbers, and strings pass through unchanged. The generated completion code imports only json and uses __import__, avoiding sys and inspect, which AppWorld's syntax safety guard forbids. No new tools, hooks, gates, or pre-submit interactions are introduced, so it should preserve the leader's behavior while reducing out-of-budget failures and non-scalar answer-normalization mismatches on unseen tasks.

This agent keeps the leader's fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and answer normalization, but makes the generated tool code self-healing without adding any new model-facing tools, hooks, or gates. `appworld_call` now resolves `apis.<app>.<api>` with attribute-or-item lookup (matching the shell's documented interface instead of assuming subscripting), caches login/authenticate tokens (access_token/auth_token/token/accessToken/authToken) in the persistent shell, and when a later call fails because a required token is missing, retries once with the cached token inside the same world interaction; if the call still fails, the same result includes that API's parameter doc so wrong arguments can be corrected without a separate docs lookup. `appworld_task` gathers each supervisor credential block independently behind lambdas, so one unavailable endpoint cannot blank the whole task context. `appworld_complete` keeps the leader's boolean/list normalization and falls back to `supervisor.complete_task(answer=...)` without `status` when the supervisor rejects that keyword. I expect this to score higher because it removes residual auth-token, wrong-argument, missing-context, and completion-signature failures in-band, without the extra interactions or fail-closed behavior that hurt earlier designs.

Keeps the leader's proven fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and answer normalization, and adds one new primitive: `appworld_batch`, a JSON-scripted declarative multi-call tool. Instead of writing error-prone Python in `appworld_execute` for straight-line sequences, the agent submits steps like `{"app":"music","api":"login","params":{...},"label":"login"}` and can pass an earlier result into a later parameter with `{"$ref":"label.path"}`; paths support both dict keys and integer list indices (for example `search.results.0.id`). All steps execute sequentially in a single world interaction, and per-step exceptions—including a failed `$ref` lookup—are caught and returned with `error_type`/`line`, so one bad call does not abort the batch and the model can retry only the failed step. This preserves the leader's behavior on tasks it already solved while reducing interaction-count pressure and Python syntax/argument mistakes on unseen multi-step tasks, which are the most likely remaining failure modes.

entries.account: This agent keeps the leader's fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and scalar answer normalization, and adds two non-intrusive improvements. First, every tool result is prefixed with the live world-call budget (e.g. [world call 4/30; 26 left]), so the model can pace long tasks, batch reads, or finish before the 30-interaction limit without spending an extra tool call to check. Second, appworld_complete accepts list/dict answers and, rather than relying only on a copied normalizer, imports AppWorld's real answer_to_text from the live appworld package, spot-checks it on a small list and None, and uses it for non-scalar answers; if that import or spot-check fails it falls back to the same conservative copied normalizer. Booleans are still converted exactly as before, and None, numbers, and strings pass through unchanged. The generated completion code imports only json and uses __import__, avoiding sys and inspect, which AppWorld's syntax safety guard forbids. No new tools, hooks, gates, or pre-submit interactions are introduced, so it should preserve the leader's behavior while reducing out-of-budget failures and non-scalar answer-normalization mismatches on unseen tasks.

entries.account: Keeps the leader's proven fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and answer normalization, and adds one new primitive: `appworld_batch`, a JSON-scripted declarative multi-call tool. Instead of writing error-prone Python in `appworld_execute` for straight-line sequences, the agent submits steps like `{"app":"music","api":"login","params":{...},"label":"login"}` and can pass an earlier result into a later parameter with `{"$ref":"label.path"}`; paths support both dict keys and integer list indices (for example `search.results.0.id`). All steps execute sequentially in a single world interaction, and per-step exceptions—including a failed `$ref` lookup—are caught and returned with `error_type`/`line`, so one bad call does not abort the batch and the model can retry only the failed step. This preserves the leader's behavior on tasks it already solved while reducing interaction-count pressure and Python syntax/argument mistakes on unseen multi-step tasks, which are the most likely remaining failure modes.

It keeps an `appworld_execute` escape hatch for arbitrary multi-step Python, but replaces the baseline's hand-written recurring snippets with validated, single-purpose tools: `appworld_task` (active task plus supervisor profile/addresses/cards/passwords), `appworld_api_docs` (app-level or single-API docs), `appworld_call` (one `apis[app][api](**params)` call), and `appworld_complete` (success/fail with typed scalar or list answers). designs.account: This agent keeps the leader's fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and scalar answer normalization, and adds two non-intrusive improvements. First, every tool result is prefixed with the live world-call budget (e.g. [world call 4/30; 26 left]), so the model can pace long tasks, batch reads, or finish before the 30-interaction limit without spending an extra tool call to check. Second, appworld_complete accepts list/dict answers and, rather than relying only on a copied normalizer, imports AppWorld's real answer_to_text from the live appworld package, spot-checks it on a small list and None, and uses it for non-scalar answers; if that import or spot-check fails it falls back to the same conservative copied normalizer. Booleans are still converted exactly as before, and None, numbers, and strings pass through unchanged. The generated completion code imports only json and uses __import__, avoiding sys and inspect, which AppWorld's syntax safety guard forbids. No new tools, hooks, gates, or pre-submit interactions are introduced, so it should preserve the leader's behavior while reducing out-of-budget failures and non-scalar answer-normalization mismatches on unseen tasks.

designs.account: Keeps the leader's proven fail-open AppWorld MCP bridge and answer normalization, and adds one new primitive: `appworld_batch`, a JSON-scripted declarative multi-call tool. Instead of writing error-prone Python in `appworld_execute` for straight-line sequences, the agent submits steps like `{"app":"music","api":"login","params":{...},"label":"login"}` and can pass an earlier result into a later parameter with `{"$ref":"label.path"}`; paths support both dict keys and integer list indices (for example `search.results.0.id`). All steps execute sequentially in a single world interaction, and per-step exceptions—including a failed `$ref` lookup—are caught and returned with `error_type`/`line`, so one bad call does not abort the batch and the model can retry only the failed step. This preserves the leader's behavior on tasks it already solved while reducing interaction-count pressure and Python syntax/argument mistakes on unseen multi-step tasks, which are the most likely remaining failure modes.

All steps execute sequentially in a single world interaction, and per-step exceptions are caught and returned with `error_type`/`line`, so one bad call does not abort the batch and the model can retry only the failed step. This preserves the leader's behavior on the tasks it already solved while reducing interaction-count pressure and Python syntax/argument mistakes on unseen multi-step tasks, which are the most likely remaining failure modes.
